primitives.name: Fielding to Plate from Third Base
primitives.verbatim_quote: The ball must be fielded to the catcher in such a manner as to enable him to touch the runner; and to field the ball thus from third base is no easy matter, as it often involves throwing the ball almost over the runner's shoulder.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'d': 'distance from third base to plate (meters)', 'v': 'throw velocity (m/s)', 'θ': "angle of throw relative to runner's path (radians)", 't': 'time to reach plate (seconds)'}
primitives.assumptions: Runner maintains constant speed, throw trajectory is ballistic, fielder's release point is fixed.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When θ approaches π/2, throw accuracy degrades due to angular momentum transfer.

layer2.mapping: Maps fielder's throw vector to catcher's ability to intercept runner using kinematic constraints derived from base distance and runner velocity.

primitives.name: Runner Advantage from Third to First
primitives.verbatim_quote: Moreover, a runner from third has an advantage of several yards over a runner to first.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'L_3to1': 'lead distance from third to first base (meters)', 'v_r': "runner's velocity (m/s)", 't_r': 'time to reach base (seconds)'}
primitives.assumptions: Base paths are straight lines, runner accelerates uniformly.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When L_3to1 < 27 meters, runner advantage becomes negligible.

layer2.mapping: Isomorphic to a time-distance trade-off model where runner advantage translates into reduced reaction time for fielders.
layer2.telemetry: Distance differential between third and first base paths

primitives.name: First Baseman Fielding Accuracy
primitives.verbatim_quote: If, however, the first baseman were obliged to touch the runner, as the catcher must do, fully one half the throws he receives would not be sufficiently accurate to enable him to execute the play.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'P_acc': 'probability of accurate throw (dimensionless)', 'σ': 'standard deviation of throw error (meters)', 'd_f': 'distance from fielder to base (meters)'}
primitives.assumptions: Throw accuracy follows normal distribution around target.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When d_f > 10 meters, P_acc drops below 0.5 due to increased error variance.

layer2.mapping: Quantifies the inverse relationship between fielder distance and throw precision in executing force plays.
layer2.telemetry: Percentage of successful throws within 0.5 meter tolerance

reasoning_traces.think:
The core tactical insight lies in the geometric and kinematic constraints of baseball fielding. When a runner advances from third to home, they benefit from a positional advantage that reduces the effective distance to the plate compared to a runner going to first. This is modeled as a function of base path length and runner velocity. Fielding from third base to plate requires a high-angle throw that risks hitting the runner, as demonstrated by Hankinson’s incident. This introduces a failure mode where physical contact negates the defensive action. The first baseman's challenge is more severe because they must touch the runner, unlike the catcher who can simply receive the ball. Thus, the probability of successful execution decreases with increasing distance from the base, forming a kernel of probabilistic failure. These primitives define a dual space: one of spatial advantage and another of mechanical precision, both governed by the same underlying kinematic principles.
